{{Short description|Functions in harmonic analysis mathematics}}
{{confused|improper integral}}
In [[mathematics]], '''singular integrals''' are central to [[harmonic analysis]] and are intimately connected with the study of partial differential equations. Broadly speaking a singular integral is an [[integral operator]]

: <math>T(f)(x) = \int K(x,y)f(y) \, dy, </math>

whose kernel function <math>K: \mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R </math> is [[Mathematical singularity|singular]] along the diagonal <math>x=y</math>.  Specifically, the singularity is such that <math>|K(x,y)|</math> is of size <math>|x-y|^{-n}</math> asymptotically as <math>|x-y| \to 0</math>. Since such integrals may not in general be absolutely integrable, a rigorous definition must define them as the limit of the integral over <math>|y-x| \to \epsilon</math> as <math>\epsilon \to 0</math>, but in practice this is a technicality. Usually further assumptions are required to obtain results such as their boundedness on [[Lp spaces]], for example <math>L^p(\mathbb R^n)</math>.

==The Hilbert transform==

{{main|Hilbert transform}}

The archetypal singular integral operator is the [[Hilbert transform]] <math>H</math>. It is given by convolution against the kernel <math>K(x)=1/(\pi x)</math> for <math>x</math> in <math>\mathbb R</math>. More precisely,

: <math>H(f)(x) = \frac{1}{\pi}\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \int_{|x-y|>\varepsilon} \frac{1}{x-y}f(y) \, dy. </math>

The most straightforward higher dimension analogues of these are the [[Riesz transform]]s, which replace <math>K(x)=1/x</math> with

: <math>K_i(x) = \frac{x_i}{|x|^{n+1}}</math>

where <math>i = 1, ..., n</math> and  <math>x_i</math> is the <math>i</math>-th component of <math>x</math> in <math>\mathbb R^n</math>. All of these operators are bounded on <math>L^p</math> and satisfy [[Hardy-Littlewood maximal function|weak-type]] <math>(1,1)</math> estimates.<ref name=bible>{{cite news | last = Stein | first = Elias | title = Harmonic Analysis | publisher = Princeton University Press| year = 1993 }}</ref>

==Singular integrals of convolution type==
{{Main|Singular integral operators of convolution type}}
A singular integral of convolution type is an operator <math>T</math> defined by convolution with a kernel <math>K</math> that is [[locally integrable function|locally integrable]] on <math>R^n\setminus \{0\}</math>, in the sense that

{{NumBlk|:|<math>T(f)(x) = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \int_{|y-x|>\varepsilon} K(x-y)f(y) \, dy. </math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

Suppose that the kernel satisfies:

# The ''size'' condition on the [[Fourier transform]] of <math>K</math>
#:<math>\hat{K}\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)</math>
# The ''smoothness'' condition: for some <math>C>0</math>,
#:<math>\sup_{y \neq 0} \int_{|x|>2|y|} |K(x-y) - K(x)| \, dx \leq C.</math>

Then it can be shown that <math>T</math> is bounded on <math>L^p(\mathbb R^n)</math> and satisfies a weak-type <math>(1,1)</math> estimate.

Property 1. is needed to ensure that convolution ({{EquationNote|1}}) with the [[distribution (mathematics)#Tempered distributions and Fourier transform|tempered distribution]] p.v.&nbsp;<math>K</math> given by the [[Cauchy principal value|principal value integral]]
:<math>\operatorname{p.v.}\,\, K[\phi] = \lim_{\epsilon\to 0^+} \int_{|x|>\epsilon}\phi(x)K(x)\,dx</math>
is a well-defined [[Fourier multiplier]] on <math>L^2</math>. Neither of the properties 1. or 2. is necessarily easy to verify, and a variety of sufficient conditions exist.  Typically in applications, one also has a ''cancellation'' condition

: <math>\int_{R_1<|x|<R_2} K(x) \, dx = 0 ,\ \forall R_1,R_2 > 0</math>

which is quite easy to check.  It is automatic, for instance, if <math>K</math> is an [[odd function]].  If, in addition, one assumes 2. and the following size condition

: <math>\sup_{R>0} \int_{R<|x|<2R} |K(x)| \, dx \leq C,</math>

then it can be shown that 1. follows.

The smoothness condition 2. is also often difficult to check in principle, the following sufficient condition of a kernel <math>K</math> can be used:
* <math>K\in C^1(\mathbf{R}^n\setminus\{0\})</math>
* <math>|\nabla K(x)|\le\frac{C}{|x|^{n+1}}</math>
Observe that these conditions are satisfied for the Hilbert and Riesz transforms, so this result is an extension of those result.<ref name = grafakos>{{Citation | last = Grafakos | first = Loukas | title = Classical and Modern Fourier Analysis | chapter = 7 | publisher = Pearson Education, Inc. | place = New Jersey| year = 2004 }}</ref>

==Singular integrals of non-convolution type==

These are even more general operators. However, since our assumptions are so weak, it is not necessarily the case that these operators are bounded on <math>L^p</math>.

===Calderón–Zygmund kernels===

A function <math>K: \mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R </math> is said to be a ''[[Alberto Calderón|Calderón]]–[[Antoni Zygmund|Zygmund]] kernel'' if it satisfies the following conditions for some constants <math>C>0</math> and <math>\delta > 0</math>.<ref name=grafakos/>
<ol type="a">
<li>
:<math>|K(x,y)| \leq \frac{C}{|x - y|^n} </math>
</li>
<li>
:<math>|K(x,y) - K(x',y)| \leq \frac{C|x-x'|^\delta}{\bigl(|x-y|+|x'-y|\bigr)^{n+\delta}}\text{ whenever }|x-x'| \leq \frac{1}{2}\max\bigl(|x-y|,|x'-y|\bigr)</math>
</li>
<li>
:<math>|K(x,y) - K(x,y')| \leq \frac{C |y-y'|^\delta}{\bigl(|x-y| + |x-y'| \bigr)^{n+\delta}}\text{ whenever }|y-y'| \leq \frac{1}{2}\max\bigl(|x-y'|,|x-y|\bigr)</math>
</li>
</ol>

===Singular integrals of non-convolution type===

<math>T</math> is said to be a ''singular integral operator of non-convolution type'' associated to the Calderón&ndash;Zygmund kernel <math>K</math> if

: <math>\int g(x) T(f)(x) \, dx = \iint g(x) K(x,y) f(y) \, dy \, dx,</math>

whenever <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are smooth and have disjoint support.<ref name=grafakos/> Such operators need not be bounded on <math>L^p</math>

===Calderón&ndash;Zygmund operators===

A singular integral of non-convolution type <math>T</math> 
associated to a Calderón&ndash;Zygmund kernel <math>K</math> 
is called a ''Calderón&ndash;Zygmund operator'' when it is bounded on <math>L^2</math>, that is, there is a 
<math>C>0</math> such that

: <math>\|T(f)\|_{L^2} \leq C\|f\|_{L^2},</math>

for all smooth compactly supported ƒ.

It can be proved that such operators are, in fact, also bounded on all <math>L^p</math> with <math>1 < p < \infty </math>.

===The <math> T(b) </math> theorem===

The <math> T(b) </math> theorem provides sufficient conditions for a singular integral operator to be a Calderón–Zygmund operator, that is for a singular integral operator associated to a Calderón–Zygmund kernel to be bounded on <math>L^2</math>. In order to state the result we must first define some terms.

A ''normalised bump'' is a smooth function <math>\varphi</math> on <math>\mathbb R^n</math> supported in a ball of radius 1 and centred at the origin such that <math>|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|<1</math>, for all multi-indices <math>|\alpha| \leq n + 2</math>. Denote by <math>\tau^x(\varphi)(y)= \varphi (y - x)</math> and <math> \varphi_r(x)=r^{-n}\varphi(x/r)</math> for all <math>x</math> in <math>\mathbb R^n</math> and <math> r > 0 </math>. An operator is said to be ''weakly bounded'' if there is a constant <math>C</math> such that

: <math> \left|\int T\bigl(\tau^x(\varphi_r)\bigr)(y) \tau^x(\psi_r)(y) \, dy\right| \leq Cr^{-n}</math>

for all normalised bumps <math>\varphi</math> and <math>\psi</math>. A function is said to be ''accretive'' if there is a constant <math>c>0</math> such that <math>Re(b)(x) \geq c</math> for all <math>x</math> in <math>\mathbb R</math>. Denote by <math>M_b</math> the operator given by multiplication by a function <math>b</math>.

The <math> T(b) </math> theorem states that a singular integral operator <math>T</math> associated to a Calderón–Zygmund kernel is bounded on <math>L^2</math> if it satisfies all of the following three conditions for some bounded accretive functions <math>b_1</math> and <math>b_2</math>:<ref>{{cite news | last = David |author3=Journé |author2=Semmes | title = Opérateurs de Calderón&ndash;Zygmund, fonctions para-accrétives et interpolation | publisher = Revista Matemática Iberoamericana | volume = 1 | pages = 1&ndash;56| language = fr | year = 1985 }}</ref>
<ol type="a">
<li><math>M_{b_2}TM_{b_1}</math> is weakly bounded;</li>
<li><math>T(b_1)</math> is in [[Bounded mean oscillation|BMO]];</li>
<li><math>T^t(b_2),</math> is in [[Bounded mean oscillation|BMO]], where <math>T^t</math> is the transpose operator of&nbsp;<math>T</math>.</li>
</ol>
